author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: Origen introduces his explanation of Paul's Epistle to the Romans with a prayer to God who teaches man knowledge. He notes that Romans is considered more difficult than Paul's other letters for two reasons: its sometimes confused and unclear expressions, and the many questions it raises, especially those heretics use to argue that each person's deeds are caused not by purpose but by diversity of nature.
argument: Origen begins by quoting Romans 10 and 15 on faith, confession, and hope. He then explains Paul's self-description as servant, called apostle, and one set apart for the gospel, distinguishing 'called' from 'elect' and stating Paul was called not by chance but according to purpose. He treats God's impartial judgment on Jews and Greeks, the true circumcision of the heart, and the justification of all through faith in Christ's blood. He discusses Abraham's justification by faith, peace with God through faith, baptism as burial with Christ into death, and the inner conflict between the law of the mind and the law of sin. Finally, he argues that not all who are from Israel are Israelites, and that election depends on God's mercy, not human will or effort.

outline.move: The opening quotes from Romans 10 and 15 set the theme of faith, confession, hope, and salvation through Christ.

Origen explains why Romans is difficult, then comments on Paul's self-description as servant, called apostle, and one set apart for the gospel, and on the revelation of God's wrath against unrighteousness.
Origen treats God's impartial judgment on Jews and Greeks and the true circumcision of the heart.
He explains that all have sinned and are justified freely through faith in Christ, whom God set forth as a propitiation.
He discusses Abraham's justification by faith, not works, and the blessedness of those whose sins are forgiven.
He treats peace with God through faith, boasting in hope, and the contrast between the one man's sin and Christ's grace.
He explains baptism as burial with Christ into death and the call to walk in newness of life, presenting one's members as instruments of righteousness.
He describes the inner conflict between the law of the mind and the law of sin, and the deliverance through Jesus Christ.
He proclaims no condemnation for those in Christ, freedom by the Spirit, and the inheritance of God's children.
He argues that not all who are from Israel are Israelites, and that election depends on God's mercy, not human will or effort.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle and author of the Epistle to the Romans, whose words Origen is explaining.

cast.name: Jesus Christ
cast.who: The Son of God, raised from the dead, through whom salvation and justification come.

cast.name: Abraham
cast.who: The patriarch whose faith was counted as righteousness, the example of justification by faith.

cast.name: Isaac
cast.who: The son of Abraham through whom the promised offspring was named.

cast.name: David
cast.who: The king from whose line Christ was born according to the flesh.

voices.speaker: Paul

key_terms.sense: Faith in Christ, the means by which justification and salvation are received
God's righteousness revealed in the gospel and given to believers through faith
The law of Moses, contrasted with faith and the Spirit as a way of justification
The Holy Spirit, through whom believers are adopted, sanctified, and freed from sin
Human flesh or the sinful human nature, contrasted with the Spirit
God's free gift of salvation and righteousness through Christ, contrasted with works
Sin as a power and condition that entered through one man and enslaves humanity
Death as the consequence of sin, both physical and spiritual
The status of being God's children through the Spirit, contrasted with slavery
God's prior determination of Christ as Son of God in power
Christ set forth by God as the atoning sacrifice that turns away wrath and shows God's justice
The inward, spiritual circumcision of the heart, contrasted with physical circumcision
Baptism as burial with Christ into his death and rising to new life
The people of God, redefined as those who are children of the promise, not merely physical descendants
False teachers who misuse Romans to argue that human actions are determined by nature, not purpose

_unresolved_facts.claim: Origen explains why Romans is difficult, then comments on Paul's self-description as servant, called apostle, and one set apart for the gospel, and on the revelation of God's wrath against unrighteousness
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Quod ceteris apostoli Pauli Epistolis difficilior putatur ad intelligendum haec quae ad Romanos scripta est, duabus mihi videtur fieri ex causis... Deprecantes Deum qui docet hominem scientiam, explanationis Epistolae Pauli ad Romanos contingemus exordium.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He proclaims no condemnation for those in Christ, freedom by the Spirit, and the inheritance of God's children
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Nihil ergo nunc damnationis est his qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Lex enim Spiritus vitae in Christo Iesu liberavit me a lege peccati et mortis. Si filii, et heredes: heredes quidem Dei, coheredes autem Christi. Expectatio creaturae revelationem filiorum Dei expectat.
_unresolved_facts.fix: He proclaims no condemnation for those in Christ, freedom by the Spirit of life from the law of sin and death, the inheritance of God's children as co-heirs with Christ, and the eager expectation of creation for the revelation of God's children
